title: How Wishful Thinking Impacts Political Polarization - Nautilus
gist: A study in Political Behavior by Seth Warner (University of Connecticut) links political polarization to wishful thinking, identifying a 'negative valence' form: partisans' belief about outcomes is driven as much by not wanting the other party to win as by wanting their own to win.

insights.claim: A recent study in Political Behavior finds that political polarization and wishful thinking — the belief that your own party will win — are related phenomena.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Partisan wishful thinking biases election expectations; poll-of-expectations and prediction-market signals may embed it.
insights.quote: on the other side of the polarization coin is wishful thinking—the belief that your party will emerge victorious—and the two phenomena are related

insights.claim: Seth Warner of the University of Connecticut identifies a previously unexplored negative valence to wishful thinking, where partisans are motivated as much by not wanting the opposing party to win as by wanting their own to win.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Negative partisanship can amplify outcome-forecast errors and market volatility around elections.
insights.quote: There’s a negative valence to wishful thinking that to this point hasn’t been explored.

insights.claim: U.S. politics has been gripped by intense political polarization for quite some time, per the author's framing on election day.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Persistent polarization raises policy-uncertainty risk premia around elections.
